items.prompt: A list gives the number of books each of $5$ students read last month: $3, 4, 4, 6, 8$. How many observations are in this data set, and what attribute is being measured?
items.answer: $n=5$ observations; the attribute is the number of books read in a month.

steps: Count the values in the list: $3, 4, 4, 6, 8$ has $5$ entries, so $n=5$.
Read the context: each value records how many books a student read last month.
So there are $n=5$ observations of the attribute number of books read per month.

items.prompt: Find the range of the ordered data set $5, 7, 9, 12, 14$.

steps: The range is the maximum value minus the minimum value: $\text{range}=\text{max}-\text{min}$.
The maximum is $14$ and the minimum is $5$.
$\text{range}=14-5=9$.

items.prompt: Find the median of the ordered data set $6, 8, 11, 13, 20$.

steps: The data is already in order and has $n=5$ values, an odd count.
The median is the single middle value, the $3$rd of $5$.
Counting in: $6, 8, \mathbf{11}, 13, 20$, the middle value is $11$.
So the median is $11$.

items.prompt: Find the mean of the data set $4, 6, 8, 10, 12$.

steps: The mean is $\bar{x}=\dfrac{\sum x_i}{n}$.
Add the values: $4+6+8+10+12=40$.
Divide by $n=5$: $\bar{x}=\dfrac{40}{5}=8$.
So the mean is $8$.

items.prompt: A week of daily high temperatures in degrees Fahrenheit is recorded as $70, 72, 68, 75, 71, 69, 74$. State the number of observations and the units of measurement.
items.answer: $n=7$ observations; the units are degrees Fahrenheit.

steps: Count the values: $70, 72, 68, 75, 71, 69, 74$ has $7$ entries, so $n=7$.
The context says each value is a daily high temperature in degrees Fahrenheit.
So there are $n=7$ observations measured in degrees Fahrenheit.

items.prompt: Find the median of the unordered data set $9, 4, 7, 7, 13$.

steps: First put the values in order: $4, 7, 7, 9, 13$.
There are $n=5$ values, an odd count, so the median is the single middle value.
The $3$rd of the $5$ ordered values is $7$: $4, 7, \mathbf{7}, 9, 13$.
So the median is $7$. (Do not use the middle of the unordered list.)

items.prompt: Find the median of the ordered data set $10, 12, 15, 19$.

steps: There are $n=4$ values, an even count, so the median is the average of the two middle values.
The two middle values are the $2$nd and $3$rd: $12$ and $15$.
Average them: $\dfrac{12+15}{2}=\dfrac{27}{2}$.
So the median is $\dfrac{27}{2}=13.5$.

items.prompt: Find the mean of the data set $5, 6, 8, 9$. Give an exact answer.

steps: The mean is $\bar{x}=\dfrac{\sum x_i}{n}$.
Add the values: $5+6+8+9=28$.
Divide by $n=4$: $\bar{x}=\dfrac{28}{4}=7$.
So the mean is $7$.

items.prompt: Find the mean of the data set $3, 4, 4, 6$. Give an exact answer as a fraction.

steps: The mean is $\bar{x}=\dfrac{\sum x_i}{n}$.
Add the values: $3+4+4+6=17$.
Divide by $n=4$: $\bar{x}=\dfrac{17}{4}$.
This does not reduce, so the exact mean is $\dfrac{17}{4}=4.25$.

items.prompt: For the ordered data set $3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12, 15, 18$, find the interquartile range (IQR).

steps: There are $n=8$ values. Split them into a lower half and an upper half of $4$ values each.
Lower half: $3, 5, 6, 8$. $Q_1$ is the median of this half: $\dfrac{5+6}{2}=\dfrac{11}{2}$.
Upper half: $9, 12, 15, 18$. $Q_3$ is the median of this half: $\dfrac{12+15}{2}=\dfrac{27}{2}$.
So the IQR is $8$.

items.prompt: Compute the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of the data set $2, 4, 6, 8$.

steps: First find the mean: $\bar{x}=\dfrac{2+4+6+8}{4}=\dfrac{20}{4}=5$.
Find each absolute deviation from the mean: $|2-5|=3$, $|4-5|=1$, $|6-5|=1$, $|8-5|=3$.
Add the absolute deviations: $3+1+1+3=8$.
Divide by $n=4$: $\text{MAD}=\dfrac{8}{4}=2$.
So the MAD is $2$. (Keep the absolute values so the deviations do not cancel to $0$.)

items.prompt: Compute the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of the data set $3, 5, 9, 11$.

steps: First find the mean: $\bar{x}=\dfrac{3+5+9+11}{4}=\dfrac{28}{4}=7$.
Divide by $n=4$: $\text{MAD}=\dfrac{12}{4}=3$.
So the MAD is $3$.

items.prompt: A dot plot of quiz scores (out of $10$) shows most dots stacked between $7$ and $9$ with a peak at $8$, and one lone dot at $1$. Describe the shape of this distribution, including any cluster, peak, gap, or outlier.
items.answer: Most scores cluster from $7$ to $9$ with a peak at $8$; the score $1$ is an outlier separated from the cluster by a gap, making the distribution skewed toward the low end.

steps: Find where most of the data sits: the dots are concentrated between $7$ and $9$, so that is the cluster.
The tallest stack is at $8$, so the peak is at $8$.
Between $1$ and $7$ there are no dots, so there is a gap in that interval.
The single value at $1$ sits far below the cluster, across the gap, so it is an outlier.
Because the lone low value stretches the data toward the small end, the distribution is skewed toward the low end (left-skewed).

items.prompt: The selling prices of $5$ houses on a street are $\$210{,}000$, $\$220{,}000$, $\$230{,}000$, $\$240{,}000$, and $\$900{,}000$. Which measure of center, the mean or the median, better describes a typical price, and why? Support your answer by computing both.
items.answer: The median, $\$230{,}000$, better describes a typical price; the mean is $\$360{,}000$, but the single very large value ($\$900{,}000$) inflates it so the mean is higher than four of the five homes.

steps: Order the prices (already ordered): $\$210{,}000, \$220{,}000, \$230{,}000, \$240{,}000, \$900{,}000$. With $n=5$ the median is the middle value, $\$230{,}000$.
Compare: the mean $\$360{,}000$ is larger than four of the five actual prices, so it is not typical.
The $\$900{,}000$ home is an outlier that pulls the mean up but barely affects the median.
So the median $\$230{,}000$ is the better summary of a typical price.

items.prompt: A data set is $6, 7, 8, 9, 40$. Find the mean. Then find the new mean after removing the outlier $40$, and explain how the outlier affects the mean.
items.answer: The mean is $14$; after removing $40$ the mean is $\frac{15}{2}=7.5$. The outlier $40$ pulls the mean up far above the other four values, so removing it drops the mean from $14$ to $7.5$.

steps: Mean of all five values: $\bar{x}=\dfrac{6+7+8+9+40}{5}=\dfrac{70}{5}=14$.
The value $40$ sits far above the cluster $6$ through $9$, so it is an outlier.
Remove $40$ and recompute with $n=4$: $\dfrac{6+7+8+9}{4}=\dfrac{30}{4}=\dfrac{15}{2}=7.5$.
Compare the two means: $14$ with the outlier versus $7.5$ without it.
The outlier raised the mean by $14-7.5=6.5$, showing that a single large value can pull the mean well above where most of the data lies.
